entry.title: The Agent Chooses
entry.content:
For an agent, every table is one step away. Only the name is left to choose by. Who decided which tables it sees?

The table that promised too much

Last week I promised to come back to r, and to who chooses when the one choosing isn’t a person. Two weeks ago, introducing this series, I drew a map with a row waiting for this story: “the agent that picks the table by its name”. Here it is: an agent that built a whole model on the wrong table, because of the table’s name.

It happened at a business conglomerate in Central America (retail and distribution): an agent built an inventory model on the wrong table. Nobody told it to. The name did.

The agent was Claude, Opus 5.5, directed by one of the junior consultants at Primus. I’m saying it up front for two reasons. It’s true, and this post is also being written with Claude. It would be strange to hide one and not the other.

The request was an inventory model: stock, cost, and the kardex behind them. Kardex is what we call the inventory ledger in Latin America: every movement that adds or takes a unit or its cost from the warehouse. In the source system there’s a table whose name, translated, is inventory_movements. Read the name again. Where would you go looking for the kardex? The agent went there too. It built silver on that table, then gold, then the semantic model, and it did a clean job: readable names, sensible relationships, measures that worked.

Then the numbers reached the semantic model, and the junior himself saw that they made no sense for the operation. Credit where it’s due: the agent didn’t catch it. The person did.

Here’s what nobody knew yet. inventory_movements doesn’t hold all the inventory movements, as it does in most ERP systems. It holds the ones no other document explains: the physical movements inside the warehouse. A sale moves inventory too. So does a purchase. A revaluation moves its value without moving a single unit. The real kardex is a UNION ALL of six tables (sales, purchases, revaluations and inventory movements among them), and it doesn’t live in any table. It lives in code. Each of those tables speaks its own dialect, too: in sales the cost sits in total_cost, which plays the role total_amount plays in purchases, and revaluations don’t use quantity at all.

In their defense, nobody thought to compare the number of sales transactions against the number of movements. Sales wasn’t even in silver. The evidence showed up in bronze, where the invoice lines outnumbered the movements by far. The truth was sitting in the one layer nobody had promoted.

The junior and Claude put together a remediation plan: rebuild the kardex in gold as a UNION ALL. It was partly right. The senior consultant on the project wasn’t sure, and it landed on my desk.

Look at what kind of mistake this is, because it isn’t the one this series has been about. inventory_movements isn’t ROT data. It’s alive, it loads every day, and every row in it is correct. Its only problem is a name that promises more than the table holds. And the right answer, the full kardex, wasn’t a table at all. It had no name. Last time I closed by saying nobody drew the map. This time the right store wasn’t even on it, and a store that isn’t on the map isn’t even one of the options. Nobody walks into it, not a person and not an agent.

One more thing, which I’ll pay off later: for the first hour, I thought the junior and Claude were the ones who had it wrong.

What I didn’t tell you about the map

Last time I told you about the red and blue dots in Guadalajara. I left one piece out, because it belongs here.

A catchment area draws customers from somewhere, and in Mexico that somewhere had a name: the AGEB. INEGI, the national statistics institute, divides the cities into Áreas Geoestadísticas Básicas, units of up to a few dozen blocks each, and publishes them in surprising detail: the polygon, plus the population and the characteristics of the housing inside it. Part of my two weeks went into reading those shapefiles, loading them into the SQL Server 2008 beta, and letting the new spatial types compute centroids, areas and distances. Our customers didn’t come from dots on a map. They came from AGEBs.

That matters because of the formula. Newton, the formula I used last time, only has one mass pulling on another. In 1963 David Huff, a geographer, wrote down what retail had been missing: a customer choosing among stores. He turned the attraction into a probability: not “this customer goes to that store” but “this customer goes to that store this often”. He writes it like this:

P(i→j) = (Aⱼ / Dᵢⱼ^β) / Σₖ (Aₖ / Dᵢₖ^β)

j is a store. A is how attractive it is. D is the distance from the customer’s origin i to the store (the r from last time, with a new letter), and β says how fast the attraction fades with that distance. The denominator adds up every store that customer could reach. What comes out isn’t a verdict, it’s a share: of the people living in i, how many end up at j.

The letter I want you to look at is i. It’s the origin, and in our model the origin was the AGEB: a centroid to measure distance from, and a census unit that told you who lived there. Once you have that, the question changes. It stops being “how attractive is this branch?” and becomes “how attractive is this branch to the people who live here?” A pawnshop doesn’t mean the same thing to every neighborhood.

(I’m taking a liberty here, and I’d rather say so. In Huff’s formula A belongs to the store, the same for everyone. Letting it depend on who’s looking is my stretch, not Huff’s.)

In data, the origin is a community of consumption: people who share a vocabulary, a set of skills and a purpose. Often that’s a department, not always. My list of what attracts a user to a model started with “names in business language”. Fine. Which business? For the warehouse, “inventory movements” means boxes moving between locations. For accounting, it means the kardex. Same name, two communities, two meanings, and both of them are right.

The lesson: attractiveness isn’t a property of the table. It’s a property of the table and whoever is looking at it.

Which leaves the question this post is really about. What happens when whoever is looking has no profile at all?

Every copy is a new store

Before I get there, one more thing the map taught me in 2008: cannibalism.

Monte de Piedad wanted 80 new branches, and the first temptation with a list like that is to put them where you already do well. The formula punishes that. Open a branch next to one of your own and the denominator grows for every customer in the area. The new branch takes share from the competition, sure, but it also takes share from your own branch down the street. You can lose customers to yourself. And in the formula, it holds for any store: a new one doesn’t have to beat the best one to hurt it. It only has to exist and look acceptable.

Now replace branches with tables. You ask for last quarter’s sales and four candidates answer to the name: sales, the certified table in gold; sales_final_v2, an analyst’s copy frozen in March; fact_sales, from the old warehouse, which stopped loading after the migration; and sales_bkp_2023, a full snapshot, the heaviest of the four. Every one of them sits in the denominator. Every one takes a piece of the probability that belonged to sales.

In the last post I said a cluster of copies adds weight without adding attraction. Here’s the other half: it competes for the attraction the good table already had. And the way it competes depends on who’s choosing.

A person who knows that business doesn’t see four tables. They see one table and three copies. “Those are the old ones.” They pick between the real one and the copies first, and only then, if at all, among the copies. Adding a fourth copy barely moves their odds. The formula doesn’t know how to do that. For Huff every alternative competes on its own, and a fourth copy takes its share from everyone, every time.

(Economists know this as the red bus / blue bus problem: add a blue bus identical to the red one and the model thinks you’ve created a new way to travel. The fix, from the seventies, is to group similar alternatives into nests and choose among nests first – the nested logit – which is exactly what the person with context does without thinking about it.)

So for the agent, every copy whose name doesn’t give it away is a new store. For the person, every copy is one more shelf in the same old store.

Which means Huff, written in 1963 to describe shoppers, doesn’t describe very well the human who knows the data. It describes the agent, facing copies with good names.

An origin with no profile

Go back to the formula and put an agent in place of the customer.

Start with D.

Madrid and Barcelona taught me what D measures. In the 2010s I made that trip dozens of times, and I almost always took the AVE, the high-speed train. On paper the plane wins: about an hour and a quarter in the air, against two and a half hours by train. But the train let me show up five minutes before departure, at a station in the middle of the city, and work from the first minute. The plane meant an airport, security, boarding, and a laptop that stayed closed until the seatbelt sign went off. (I took the Puente Aéreo, the no-reservation shuttle, exactly once.)

I wasn’t the exception. Since the AVE opened in 2008, it has taken most of that market from the plane, about three passengers in four by 2023, without shortening a single kilometer. What it shortened was the effort.

Remember the Excel file on my laptop, the asteroid that pulls harder than the lakehouse because it’s right there. For a person, distance is effort, and effort can play either way: it keeps the old Excel file close, and the dead table far. For the agent, that distance disappears. Everything in the schema it was given is one step away. No ticket, no search, no colleague to ask. D goes to one for every table, and β goes with it: whatever its value, one to any power is still one. The only thing left in the formula is A. (When the schema is too big and the agent searches it first, D comes back, as a search ranking. And the ranking is decided by the same thing: the name and the description.)

A person pays for r in payroll. The agent doesn’t pay in distance. Every table in its scope is one more thing to read, ROT data included, so it pays in tokens, and in wrong answers.

In the last post I said attraction is what makes you walk over, and light is what you find when you get there. ROT data has the first and not the second. A person who gets to fact_sales might notice the dates stop last year. The agent doesn’t look. It reads the label and gets to work.

Then look at i: an origin with no profile. It doesn’t belong to the warehouse or to accounting. It doesn’t know which tables “are the old ones”. It judges attractiveness from the only thing it can see, the schema: the names, the columns and, if someone wrote one, the description. In other words, by the average of what a name means to anyone, and that’s the ground where ROT data competes best.

There’s evidence that the name carries a lot of weight. Researchers took a standard text-to-SQL benchmark and rewrote the questions, swapping the words that pointed at tables and columns for natural synonyms, nothing else, and the models’ accuracy dropped by roughly 20 to 30 points. (Gan and colleagues, ACL 2021, the Spider-Syn paper. Their phrase is that the models “rely on the lexical matching” between the question and the schema.)

That’s the failure from one side: take the matching name away and they get lost. Turn it around and you get the kardex: give the wrong table the matching name, and the same reliance sends the agent straight to it.

To be fair, the newer models are better at this than that paper suggests. A 2024 study found that strong reasoning models can pick out the relevant schema even when you hand them a lot of irrelevant tables (Maamari and colleagues, “The Death of Schema Linking?”). I believe it. But irrelevant isn’t the problem. bkp_customers_old is irrelevant, and any decent model throws it away. fact_sales isn’t irrelevant. It answers the question. It just answers it with last year’s data.

Remember the list from the last post: ROT data can match the good data on five of six attributes – the names, ease of navigation, metadata, quality, hidden complexity – and the one it can’t fake is relevance, which doesn’t show up in the schema. The agent judges exactly those five, from the schema alone. Microsoft’s own guidance for Fabric data agents says as much in plain words: don’t put archived staging tables in the agent’s scope, and if two of the objects you selected hold similar data, tell the agent which one is authoritative. In their words: “Don’t rely on naming alone.”

The wrong profile

Now the hour I promised.

When the senior brought me the remediation plan, I read it and thought the junior and Claude had gotten lost. In my head inventory_movements was the kardex. I didn’t have to think about it. I studied economics, I spent my first working years in administration, and for anyone who grew up near accounting, “inventory movements” means every entry that changes the quantity or the value of what’s on the shelf. That’s the kardex. In that system, it means boxes moving inside the warehouse.

I had the same reading as the agent. Worse: the agent was guessing from the name, with no profile. I had a profile, from another community, and it made me sure. The agent’s guess can be caught by someone who looks at the numbers. My certainty had to be caught by me.

What changed my mind wasn’t an argument. It was a pattern. In every inventory model I’ve built, the kardex is at least as long as sales and purchases put together, because every invoice line moves something off a shelf or onto one. So I went back to bronze and profiled the data myself, and I didn’t need more than the row counts. For the operation of a company that size, the table had far too few rows. Next to sales and purchases, it wasn’t even close. That ended the hour.

The rest was confirmation. I took the numbers to the client’s IT team, and they agreed: inventory_movements only held the warehouse’s own movements. Later, when I got access to their code, I found the UNION ALL. The kardex had been there all along. It just lived in code, where no map could see it.

The lesson: no profile is a risk. The wrong profile can be a bigger one, because it doesn’t feel like a guess.

Once I saw it, the junior and Claude had the what right. The kardex needed to exist as something with a name. Where I disagreed was the where. Their plan built it in gold, inside one model, and I want business rules to live in silver, defined once, so data scientists, agents and gold can all reuse them instead of each of them rebuilding the logic in a schema that fits only their own use. So the concept went to silver, in the business vault: built once, not ingested, with views for the data scientists and for the gold star schema. Bronze didn’t change.

That’s the part I care about more than the modeling. A UNION ALL hidden in code has zero attractiveness, because it has no name. Giving it a name puts the right store on the map. And where you put it matters: in gold, it’s the private knowledge of one model. In silver, every community – warehouse, accounting, the next agent – walks past the same door.

Anthropic found the same thing from the inside, in the article I recommended before this series started. They gave their agent grep access to thousands of SQL files, every piece of prior work they had, and accuracy moved less than a point: “our bottleneck wasn’t access to prior work, it was structure.” The kardex had been in code all along. Code isn’t a name.

The ROT data version, with numbers

The kardex was the case where the right answer had no name. In my experience, ROT data is the more common case: I rarely meet a company with an archival plan. And it’s the worse one: the right answer has a name, and so do three impostors.

Here are the four sales tables again, with numbers. A warning before you look: this is a mental model, not a measurement. The scores are made up, and nobody has calibrated Huff for tables. I set β to 1. In Huff it’s estimated from data, and 1 is the conservative choice here: a steeper decay, say Newton’s square, only widens the gap. The person goes to 76%, the agent doesn’t move. The point is the shape, not the decimals.

Table What it really is Person with context: A / D Agent: A (schema only), D = 1
sales Gold, certified. The right one 8 / 1 = 8 4 (“sales table”, generic)
sales_final_v2 Analyst’s copy, frozen in March 2 / 1 = 2 (it’s in their workspace) 3 (“final” sounds definitive)
fact_sales Old warehouse, stopped loading 0.5 / 2 = 0.25 (“that one’s dead”) 3.5 (fact_ looks official)
sales_bkp_2023 Full snapshot, the heaviest 1.5 / 2 = 0.75 0.5 (“bkp” gives it away)
Chance of the right pick   8 / 11 = 73% 4 / 11 = 36%

I’m using Huff for both columns so they’re comparable. For the person, D is effort: 1 for anything in a workspace they already open, 2 for the old warehouse and the archive, which they’d have to go find. The real person does better than 73%: they nest, and the copies barely register. The agent’s 36% is what Huff actually predicts.

Set the person’s D to 1 and they still get 67% (8 out of 12). Distance isn’t what separates them. The profile is.

Look at the bottom row and then at the heaviest table. The backup, the one that weighs the most, is the least dangerous: its name gives it away. The dangerous one is fact_sales, small and attractive. The dangerous ROT data isn’t the heavy one. It’s the attractive one. Mass explains the cost and the exposure; attraction explains the other risk.

Now the levers, same made-up numbers, applied to the agent:

What you do Agent’s chance of the right pick
Nothing 36%
Say sales is certified where the agent reads it: its description (A from 4 to 8) 53%
Also mark fact_sales as deprecated (A from 3.5 to 0.5) 67%
Take fact_sales and the backup out of the agent’s scope 73%
Retire sales_final_v2 too (only sales is left) 100%

Certifying and deprecating get the agent from 36 to 67, and stop there. That’s ranking: the bad table is still in the race, just further back. Getting to the person’s 73% takes eligibility: taking things out of scope, so the impostors never enter the denominator. Anthropic’s version is structural: for their canonical datasets, “the agent is structurally routed to them first”, by tooling, by CI and by mandate.

The 100% is the model being trivial: one store, nothing to choose. It lasts exactly as long as the scope does. Hand the agent all of silver instead of the doors you chose for it, and the denominator fills up again. The scope is a decision with an owner, not a setting.

The vendors are building those first two. Fabric shows endorsed items with a badge and lists them first in some places; Databricks lets you mark a table certified or deprecated and says that helps Genie One prioritize the assets your organization vouches for; and plenty of catalog search tools rank results by popularity. Useful, all of them. But notice the last one: if everyone uses sales_final_v2, popularity pushes it up. A ranking by use rewards attractive ROT data.

And it gets worse with time. Say sales_final_v2 was the right table for six months, and everyone learned to use it. Then sales_final_v3 shows up. What should the agent do? By name, v3 looks newer, so a curious agent jumps to it the day it appears, validated or not. By popularity, v2 stays on top for months after it stopped being right. Neither signal answers the question, because the answer is a decision: who certified v3, and when v2 retires. A version suffix is a decision nobody wrote down.

Copies aren’t the only impostors. Time makes them too: last year’s rows, still sitting in the right table. Those take deleting, and deleting doesn’t have to be final. In the last few years I’ve stopped writing gold SLAs as “data since 2020”. A fixed start date is a contract that fills up with ROT data a little more every year. I write them as a window instead, usually the last five to seven calendar years. On January 1, 2027, the load stops bringing 2020 into gold and removes what was there. The layer underneath doesn’t change: silver, the data vault and the business vault, or the warehouse, when the architecture is a warehouse with data marts on top. The marts get the same window. The history stays where it’s governed. It just leaves the shelf where users and agents shop.

Anthropic marks deprecated models in its lineage graph, and as far as their article says, it doesn’t delete them. Marking something old is a decision anyone can make. Deleting it needs an owner, and so does any cut that takes something off the shelf without deleting it. Last time, the customer table got one: the product owner signed a subset for receivables. Nothing deleted, and the same eligibility move, made for a model instead of an agent.

Your Monday worksheet

Probability of a right pick. Twenty minutes, one question.

  1. Pick a question your users or your agent get asked often. “Sales last quarter” works.
  2. List every table or dataset whose name would answer it. Include every version, not only the latest.
  3. Give each one an A from 0 to 10, twice: once as someone who knows the business, once reading only the schema.
  4. For the person column, give each a D from 1 to 3 (1 = already in my workspace, 2 = I’d have to go find it, 3 = I’d need a ticket). The agent’s D is 1, unless it searches the schema first; then score the search, not the distance.
  5. Compute each table’s A/D, and the right one’s share in both columns.
  6. Decide per row: make its certification visible, deprecate it, take it out of the agent’s scope, or retire it. Score again.
  7. Before you trust any table, do the check nobody did in the kardex case: compare its row count against something whose size you already know. Invoice lines against movements would have caught it in five minutes.

My rule of thumb: if, by your own scores, the agent is more likely to pick a wrong table than the right one (under 50% in the agent column), don’t point an agent at that area yet. The number is as rough as your scores. The comparison isn’t.

And one question the worksheet can’t answer for you: when you scored “as someone who knows the business”, which business were you?

Who decided what the agent sees?

The agent built a model on inventory_movements because the name promised it. Who decided that the kardex would live in code, with no name, where nothing could choose it? Who decided which tables the agent would see, and which of them it would believe? Nobody. Somebody handed it a schema, and the names did the rest.

In 2008 the map had every branch on it, and the people who knew the business argued over it. In that conglomerate the right store wasn’t on the map, and the only one arguing was a junior who looked at the numbers and didn’t believe them. He was right. I needed an hour to catch up.

One last thing, because it’s the next post. Suppose that, to help the next agent, someone asks an LLM to write the description of inventory_movements. I’m fairly sure what it would write: “Contains all inventory movements.” The next agent would read it and believe it, this time with a description to back it up. Who wrote that description?

This is the second of ten posts in Who Decided That? The cloud and AI made it cheap to create, copy and keep data. They didn’t make it any cheaper to decide.
entry.summary: For an agent, every table is one step away. Only the name is left to choose by. Who decided which tables it sees?

entry.title: The ROT Weighs
entry.content:
Redundant, obsolete and trivial data has mass. The cloud keeps it, and nobody decided to.

Last week I said the reader changed. Before we get to the new reader, I want to look at what it reads: the mass that piles up around the good data, and that nobody decided to keep.

2008, Mexico City

In 2008 I spent two weeks in Mexico City building a proof of concept for Nacional Monte de Piedad, the pawn institution that has been lending money against jewelry, watches and household goods in Mexico since 1775. Microsoft co-funded it. The goal was to show two things SQL Server 2008 was bringing to market: data mining and the new geospatial types. Monte de Piedad brought the business question. They planned to open 80 branches in three years, and they wanted to know where.

The question sounds simple. It isn’t. It’s a classic problem of spatial analysis, the discipline that studies how location shapes behavior, and in retail it has its own name: site selection. Where a new branch will get its customers depends on how big it is, how far people are willing to travel, and who is already open down the street. Retail geography answered that question almost a century ago by borrowing from physics: a store pulls customers the way a mass pulls another mass. The bigger the store, the stronger the pull. The farther away the customer, the weaker it gets. I wasn’t a retail geographer. Before those two weeks in Mexico I spent about six months reading that literature, trying to understand why stores attract, how the pull fades with distance, and why competitors cluster on the same street instead of spreading out.

With that in hand, we built a database: the location of every branch in the country, ours and the competition’s, and the commercial performance of Monte de Piedad’s own branches. Later came the points of interest around each one. On top of it we wrote views that did the geospatial math, and those views trained the data mining models. What came out the other end was a Virtual Earth map. Red dots for Monte de Piedad, blue dots for the competition. Around each branch the model drew a catchment area: the zone a branch pulls its customers from, wider when the branch is bigger, fading the farther away the customer lives. Where blue dots clustered with no red dot nearby, we had a candidate zone. Competitors in a cluster pull more together than they would apart, and Monte de Piedad wasn’t there to get any of that pull. Worse, it was leaving that market to the competition.

One of the views from the national study: Guadalajara. Red, Monte de Piedad; blue, the competition. The blue cluster at the bottom center is a strong candidate zone.

The model didn’t decide anything. It drew a map for the people who knew the business. My part ended with the POC; Microsoft turned it into videos and demos, and I never learned where Monte de Piedad finally opened its branches, or with which model.

What stayed with me was the gravity. It was my first encounter with a gravity model outside physics: Newton’s equation, written for planets, with square meters where the mass goes and kilometers where the distance goes. And it described a street in Guadalajara well enough to argue over where to put real money. Not perfectly. Well enough. Since then I’ve believed, and I have no way to prove it, that gravity is more universal than physics: whatever accumulates pulls, and whatever is far away pulls less. I kept the screenshot and gave sessions on the SQL behind the map. And for all that belief, in my head it was a business tool. It never crossed my mind to point it at my own work, at the tables behind the map, which had a gravity of their own.

I had gravity in my hands, and I didn’t see that data has mass too.

Someone else saw it

I read Dave McCrory’s “Data Gravity” years after he published it on his blog, in December 2010. I nodded, and I forgot it. I never used the term with a client.

This year a friend brought it back. Adrian Miranda Cordero’s article “Control de costos en la nube: cuando la elasticidad se convierte en el problema” (Cloud cost control: when elasticity becomes the problem) puts data gravity first on his list of patterns behind cloud bills that grow while the business doesn’t. This time the idea landed, because I had something to set it against: ROT data, data that is Redundant, Obsolete or Trivial. The tension between those two, data gravity and ROT data, is what lit this post. Each one, on its own, explained half of what I see in today’s data platforms. I needed them pulling against each other.

McCrory’s definition, in his words:

“Consider Data as if it were a Planet or other object with sufficient mass. As Data accumulates (builds mass) there is a greater likelihood that additional Services and Applications will be attracted to this data.”

McCrory asked us to treat data as a planet, so let’s take him at his word and use Newton:

g = G · M / r²

g is the pull you feel, M is the mass (call it gigabytes), r is the distance. I’m leaving G alone. It’s a constant, and the moment you start mapping physical constants onto IT, a useful metaphor turns into pseudoscience.

Look at what’s in the equation, and what isn’t. There’s no V (Value). A petabyte of duplicated snapshots pulls your architecture exactly as hard as a petabyte of general ledger balances or transactions. And mass adds up: two bodies close together pull like one. Hold on to that. It comes back later.

I want to make the comparison explicit, because it runs through this whole series. In 2008 we drew the map of a city. Here we’re drawing the map of your data platform. The equation doesn’t change. What each letter measures does:

  Site selection, 2008 Your data platform
What pulls A branch A table, a model, a dataset
Mass (M) Square meters Gigabytes
Who gets pulled A customer A user, a report, a pipeline
Distance (r) Kilometers from home to the branch The effort to reach the data

Now picture your data platform the way McCrory asked us to, as a solar system. The lakehouse is a gas giant, and the warehouse next to it is another one. Around them orbit the data marts, smaller planets with moons of their own. And everywhere there are asteroids: the Excel files on everyone’s laptop. Each one pulls with its mass.

Two different things pull here. Mass pulls the architecture: services, pipelines, backups, cost. It doesn’t care about value. What pulls a user is something else, and we’ll get to it.

By mass, the lakehouse should win every time. It doesn’t. The Excel file on my machine weighs almost nothing, but it’s right there: I double-click and I’m in. The lakehouse is enormous, and it’s far. I have to find the right workspace, request access, wait for someone to approve it, work out which of forty tables is the one, and then learn what the columns mean. That’s r. Not kilometers, not milliseconds. Effort.

And in Newton r is squared. I won’t defend the exponent for effort, but the shape is right: distance doesn’t just weaken the pull, it crushes it. That’s how the Excel file on my laptop pulls me harder than a lakehouse with a hundred thousand times its data. And notice what nobody checks when the closest planet wins: whether the Excel file is still true. Often it’s last month’s export.

The cloud doesn’t delete. It gives you a discount.

In April 2011, four months after “Data Gravity”, McCrory published “Defying Data Gravity”, ten strategies to live with heavy data, from caching and replication to compression. Every one of them moves the data, copies it, hides it, or brings the application closer. McCrory never says it this way, but most of them are playing with r. None of them deletes anything. That’s not a criticism: he was solving latency, not governance. A year later he even named the incentive that made it worse, artificial data gravity: inbound transfer to S3 and Azure was free. Putting data in got cheaper on purpose. Deciding what to do with it didn’t.

Adrian Miranda reads the same gravity through cost. Data, he writes, “gravitates and accumulates”, a property applications don’t have: “An application server can be restarted every night without a second thought” (my translation). A data platform can’t. His storage sprawl is a list I recognized right away: historical data online by default with no retention policy, execution logs kept forever, redundant backups. That’s ROT data, the O and the R, described without the name. One of his questions for a technology director is the bridge to this post: “How much historical data is online that hasn’t been queried in the last six months?” He brings the cost. I want to add the risk.

Every row you keep is something you have to protect, something an auditor can ask you about, and something that can leak. A customer’s name, tax ID and phone number are value and liability in the same record. Most privacy laws say the same thing in different words: keep personal data only as long as the purpose that justified collecting it is still alive. When the data is relevant, the value pays for the risk. When it’s ROT data, you carry the risk and nobody collects the value. That part never shows up on the cloud bill.

There’s one more cost that never shows up on the cloud bill, and it’s r. Every ROT table in the lakehouse is one more place someone has to look, one more “which of these is the right one?”, one more message to the colleague who might know. ROT data doesn’t only weigh. It pushes the good data farther away. Your cloud provider doesn’t bill you for that effort. You pay it in payroll, by the hour, to people who were hired to use the data, not to go looking for it.

Fifteen years after McCrory’s list, the tools still sit in the same place. Cloud storage has lifecycle rules that can delete, and in the projects I’ve worked on they almost never get turned on for curated data.

So most of the time the cloud doesn’t delete. It gives you a discount. Hot to cool, cool to archive, a smaller line on the invoice, and the data stays exactly where it was in your architecture, still pulling.

And there’s a deeper problem. Storage decides by file and by date. ROT data lives in rows and in meaning.

The name

If the cloud doesn’t delete, who does? It has to be someone who can read rows and meaning, not files and dates. But before anyone can look for it, the thing they’re looking for needs a name.

I found the term this year, studying for the CDMP. The DMBOK2 (DAMA’s Data Management Body of Knowledge, 2nd edition) uses it exactly once, in chapter 1, among the implications of the data lifecycle (§2.5.9):

“Data Management efforts should focus on the most critical data: Organizations produce a lot of data, a large portion of which is never actually used. Trying to manage every piece of data is not possible. Lifecycle management requires focusing on an organization’s most critical data and minimizing data ROT (Data that is Redundant, Obsolete, Trivial) (Aiken, 2014).”

That’s all of it. (The DMBOK credits Aiken; I’m quoting the DMBOK, not him.) Three sentences were enough to hook me. Nobody seems to know who coined the term. It has been around since at least the early 2000s, and it’s at home in records management and information governance, two worlds BI barely talks to. That’s how I spent 25 years in BI without hearing it.

Back in the DMBOK, chapter 9 (Document and Content Management) has the psychology, without the acronym. One of its reasons organizations don’t remove non-value-added information: “Perceived cost of making a decision and removing physical and electronic records.” The cost of making a decision. That’s the subtitle of this series, sitting in the DMBOK.

The odd part is that I had described ROT data before I knew its name. On Halloween 2017 I wrote a post for the Primus Data blog called “La bodega de datos zombis” (The zombie data warehouse). The zombie warehouse moves, with daily or weekly loads, but the movement is automatic: “The Zombie-DW is an automaton that cannot explain why certain processes or tasks are done, nor what the value of the stored information is.” And like any zombie it feeds on its own kind: it “burns valuable resources” in IT maintenance and support (my translation, both). That’s Adrian’s cost, nine years early. In 2017 I called it a zombie. In 2026 I found out it already had a name. Less cinematic than mine, but fair enough: zombies do rot.

The same post had a sentence I saw come true again about a year ago, at a client: “even having users, this model can be a zombie, because the warehouse’s customers use it like automatons.” On a project for a large company I was responsible for one tabular model, and while checking adoption I left the filter open to see all the others. In two of them, the most active user was the developer, running weekly regression tests that compared production metrics against the new version. After eight years in production, the only “adoption” those models had was the developer’s own proof that they were still alive. The zombie was generating its own usage. The technology had changed completely since 2017. The behavior hadn’t.

Back to Mexico: Newton wasn’t enough

Back to the map. Our first iteration in Mexico was exactly the formula above, with M in square meters of branch. It wasn’t enough, for two reasons.

The first one is agglomeration. Pawnshops cluster. Five of them on the same avenue don’t behave like five small masses; customers read the street as the place you go to pawn something, and the cluster pulls harder than the five of them added up. That blue group at the bottom of the Guadalajara map is exactly that.

Remember I asked you to hold on to “mass adds up”? This is where Newton falls short, in Mexico and in data. Data agglomerates too, but what attracts is different things that belong together. Customers, purchases and products, each on its own, attract very few users. Put them together, a purchase pointing to a customer and a product, and they answer questions none of them could answer alone. The attraction jumps. In a corporation, the customers of one company attract a few users. The customers of every company, integrated in silver, attract far more.

Now cluster customer, customer_v2 and customer_old instead. They can weigh exactly the same as the integrated set. They don’t attract the same. Five pawnshops on one avenue are five real offers to compare. Three copies of the customer table are one offer and two echoes.

Picture a food court. It works because it’s agglomeration done right: tacos, sushi, pizza and a Costa Rican casado, different offers that pull harder together than the four of them added up. Now picture one where ten counters sell the same menu. One still has last year’s prices, another has a dish crossed out with tape, and nobody tells you which kitchen is still cooking. You don’t have ten options. You have one, and the job of figuring out which line to stand in.

ROT data adds to the weight of the good data, and you pay for that weight. It adds nothing to what that data can tell you.

The second reason: size alone didn’t explain attraction. Two branches of the same size didn’t pull the same. So we added what was around each one (transit stops, schools, parks, churches) and let a decision tree tell us which of those mattered. Attraction turned out to have several attributes, and it was the data, not our intuition, that picked them.

Data models have attributes too, but nobody has run that decision tree for them, not that I know of. So the list below comes from the only source I have: years of watching people adopt one model and ignore the one next to it. It’s mine, from field work, not from a paper. Take it as a first attempt:

Attribute What it means in a data model
Names in business language “Net Sales”, not amt_net_lcl. The user recognizes what they’re looking at.
Easy to navigate Few tables, clear relationships. You find what you need without a map.
Explanatory metadata Descriptions that tell you what a measure includes and what it leaves out.
Quality The numbers are right, and they reconcile with the books.
Hides technical complexity Surrogate keys, staging columns and load flags stay out of sight.
Relevance (signal, not noise) It answers a question the business is asking today.

That’s the something else I promised: what attracts a user to a model isn’t its size. It’s these six. Now ask the uncomfortable question: can an old copy, the model nobody retired, attract the same way? Go down the list. The names: yes, a copy inherits them. Easy to navigate: yes, and the old model is often the simpler one. The metadata: yes, the descriptions got copied too, or were written back when they were true. Quality, the way most people check it: yes. The data was correct once, it still is, and it still reconciles with the books it came from. The one quality dimension it fails is timeliness, and nobody checks timeliness when they’re picking a model. What died is the context. Hiding complexity: yes, age has nothing to do with it. Relevance: no.

ROT data can win on five of six. The one it can’t fake is relevance: the obsolete and the trivial don’t have it, and the redundant only has it on loan from the original. That much is just the definition. What matters is that the other five, the ones you can see, can’t tell you which is which. And relevance doesn’t show up in the schema.

Dark matter: weight without light

Astronomers ran into this problem too, at a much bigger scale. Galaxies move too fast for the mass you can see. The stars at their edges orbit as if something were holding them, and with only what shines, they should fly apart. Newton, counting only the visible mass, doesn’t add up. So there has to be mass nobody can see: dark matter. It pulls like any other mass, but it doesn’t emit, absorb or reflect light. (The more academic readers will recognize Fritz Zwicky, who called it dunkle Materie in 1933, and Vera Rubin, whose galaxy rotation curves in the 1970s made it hard to ignore.)

That’s ROT data. It counts in the gravity. It keeps backups, pipelines and a developer’s regression tests in orbit, and it shows up on the bill. Your platform behaves as if it were much heavier than the data you actually use, and that’s the clue that it’s there. But it gives off no light, and by light I mean information that supports decisions. Attraction is what makes you walk over. Light is what you find when you get there. ROT data can borrow attraction, five attributes out of six. Once you’re there, it has nothing to show you. No light is a verdict about a purpose, though: not everything dark is ROT data, and that’s a post of its own.

The lesson: ROT data has mass and no light. Mass explains the cost, and the exposure. The other risk is what happens when it attracts anyway: someone, or something, picks it, and decides in the dark.

Drawing the map of a customer table

Relevance doesn’t show up in the schema. You have to measure it.

Recently I worked on an accounts receivable model for a client. The plan was the obvious one: use the same customer dimension every other model already used. A conformed dimension, in Kimball’s language. And here’s a misreading I see all the time: people take conformed to mean the same data. It doesn’t. Conformed means the same column names, the same attribute meanings and the same domain values, so a customer looks the same in every model that touches it. The rows can be identical to the full dimension, or a subset of it (for the purists, that’s Kimball’s conformance test, and it accepts both). The default is identical. Nobody asks.

Then I profiled the table, and I couldn’t make sense of it. Electronic invoicing had been mandatory for a long time. Why was a customer table this dirty? Whole blocks of strange tax IDs and odd names.

It took me a while to see it. The data wasn’t dirty. It was old. Some context, if your country doesn’t have this: in Costa Rica, an electronic invoice goes to the tax authority, which validates it, and it has to name a customer the tax authority can identify. Before it became mandatory, the old system stored whatever name the customer gave at the register, with an ID number nobody could trust. After it, a customer was someone the tax authority could find. The meaning of “customer” changed, and nobody went back to mark the records from the old regime.

Last week I wrote that meaning comes first. In that distributor, nobody had decided what a customer was. Here somebody had, and then the meaning moved, and the old records stayed where they were. Deciding once isn’t enough. Somebody has to go back.

When I measured it, about two out of every three customers in that table were ROT records. Most of the rest were good records that had nothing to do with receivables: real customers, valid IDs, no balances, no collections. The customers that actually mattered to receivables were about 4% of the table.

Those two-thirds didn’t rot with age. They rotted in one block, the day the rules changed. They’re obsolete by regime change, not by date. No rule based on creation dates would ever find them, because they aren’t files. They’re rows in a live table.

“Delete them, then.” No. The historical invoices point at those customers. There’s the gravity: correct invoices holding on to dead customers. Delete the customer and you break the invoice. And the DMBOK warns about disposing too early just as clearly as about keeping too long: some of what looks like ROT data is the record you’ll need the day after an audit.

The risk was real too, even though it never showed up on an invoice. The default sent the personal data of the whole table, names and tax IDs included, into every model, for a purpose that needed 4% of it. Nobody had approved that exposure. Nobody had been asked.

So I drew the map. If you run it on your own data on Monday, remember: it isn’t a tool for deleting. It’s for deciding.

It has two axes, and it should work on any entity with a business process behind it, not only customers.

The first axis is activity: the last business event of the process, inside a window you choose. Age is measured from the last activity, never from creation. That’s how the regime change shows up: the old records were created on a thousand different days, so creation date can’t find them. The ones that rotted went quiet once the rules changed. The ones that kept moving stay, with a label. You write the exceptions down explicitly: what’s legal or vital stays, whatever its activity. In the receivables model, accounts in legal collection got a much longer window than everything else.

One rule before you measure activity, courtesy of the zombie with one user: don’t count the activity your own systems generate. For a model, that’s the developer’s regression tests and the account that refreshes it. For a customer, it can be a lot louder. In 2008, at a retailer in Brazil, a monitoring robot logged into the website and placed an order every five minutes, invoice included, so it could raise an alert if the site or the invoicing went down. By invoice count, it was probably their most loyal customer. Activity means the business did something.

The second axis is verification, in three states: verified by an external authority (for us, the tax authority), valid format but unverified, and invalid. For most entities, the verification column needs a different authority; sometimes it’s your own master data.

(For the data quality people: invalid fails validity, verified passes accuracy, and timeliness is the activity axis’s job.)

  Verified Valid format, unverified Invalid
With activity Keep. Labeled verified Keep. Labeled unverified Keep. Labeled invalid
No activity Pseudonymized historical record Pseudonymized historical record Pseudonymized historical record

Look at what each axis decides. Activity decides whether the record stays identified. Verification decides nothing: it becomes metadata the user can see. It’s tempting to filter out the invalid IDs, or put them in quarantine. Don’t. An active customer with an invalid ID isn’t noise. It’s a signal: someone has to fix that record, and collections wants to know before they call. That’s the “explanatory metadata” attribute from the table above, doing its job.

With the map on the table, there were two cuts. The first one in the full customer dimension, the one every model uses: customers with no activity became pseudonymized historical records. The invoices still point at someone; nobody’s name or tax ID rides along anymore. (Pseudonymized, not anonymized: the tax ID is hashed with a salt we keep, so it could be reversed. We don’t.) That cut didn’t need my argument. The data protection law already asked for it, and the records from before electronic invoicing were nobody’s idea of an asset. The second one only for receivables: a dimension that conforms to the full one, same names, same meanings, same values, carrying only the customers with credit and something to collect. A cash customer is real and alive. For receivables, it’s trivial. Nothing deleted. How we built it deserves its own post later in this series; the principle fits in one line: the mass stays, the exposure goes.

The product owner signed the second one. For the wrong reasons. I was arguing governance; the business heard performance. Going from the whole table to about one customer in twenty-five changes how a model behaves, especially when the customer dimension carries dozens, even hundreds, of attributes. The model got faster, and that’s what sold it.

I’ll take it. A right decision for the wrong reason is still a decision. But think about what it means: if the model had been fast enough, nobody would have signed anything, and receivables would still be carrying the whole table to collect from 4% of it.

The lesson: whether something is ROT data gets decided by relevance, not by quality. And someone has to decide it.

Nobody drew the map

In 2008 I never found out who decided where the 80 branches went. But there was a map, and the people who knew the business had it in front of them.

Nobody ever drew the map of that customer table. Two out of every three customers rode into every model for years, and not because someone decided they should. Nobody had put the dots on a map. When someone finally did, the decisions got made: one because the law required it, the other for a reason I wouldn’t have picked.

So, how much of your data gravity is ROT data? And who decided that?

Next time we’ll come back to r, and to who chooses when the one choosing isn’t a person.

This is the first of ten posts in Who Decided That? The cloud and AI made it cheap to create, copy and keep data. They didn’t make it any cheaper to decide.
entry.summary: Redundant, obsolete and trivial data has mass. The cloud keeps it, and nobody decided to.

entry.title: The Reader Changed
entry.content:
I closed Trust Erosion saying the fix is a better reader. Then the reader changed: now it’s an AI agent, and it doesn’t ask questions.

A puppy named Hugo

October 8, 2026. I was watching Data Hero Summit 2026, Profisee’s virtual event, from my desk in Costa Rica. I don’t sell Profisee and have no relationship with the company. Malcolm Hawker, their Chief Data Officer, gave the keynote, What Is Trust Made Of. He works with some of the largest companies in the world. I work with mid-sized companies in Central America. We’ve never met, and he was describing the data platforms I see every week.

The audio failed for the first few minutes, so what I have from the opening is a screenshot. A puppy in comic-book style, a black-and-white terrier with big eyes, and a speech bubble: “Your new AI agent. Knows a lot about a lot of things. About your business? Practically nothing.” His name is Hugo. (Hugo is also an acronym on the slide – Harmonize, Unify, Govern, Orchestrate. That’s the vendor part, and I’ll leave it there.)

I didn’t need the audio. Hugo is ungrounded. He’ll bring you something every time you throw the ball, with total enthusiasm, and he has no way of knowing whether it was the ball.

A few slides later the sound was back, and so was Hugo’s work: “The answers looked perfect. And they were quietly, confidently wrong.”

I smiled. A week earlier I had closed a series on that same idea, minus the dog. Nobody borrowed from anybody. When someone looking at global corporations and someone looking at a distributor in Costa Rica describe the same failure on their own, it stops being an opinion. It’s how modern data platforms work now.

The fix I proposed

Trust Erosion ended on October 1st. Ten posts taking apart numbers that lied: a definition everyone signed and nobody shared, a table that stopped matching its concept, a sum of things that couldn’t be summed, a metric gamed for a bonus. I closed the series with one sentence, and I still believe it: the fix was never a better number. The fix is a better reader. The engineers who interrogated the sensor before trusting it. The analyst who asks what the dashboard is wired to.

Hugo doesn’t ask questions. An agent has no posture. It doesn’t feel the small discomfort you feel when a number is too round, and it can’t tell that a reading should bother it. It reads labels and fetches.

So my fix has a problem. The reader changed.

Hawker said it better than I would have: “AI didn’t create this problem. AI is magnifying it.” I’ve been saying the same thing from the other end for years: every technology wave gives us a fresh chance to repeat the same old mistakes. This wave repeats them faster, at scale, with perfect formatting.

Why the source matters

The center of the keynote was an article Anthropic published on June 3: How Anthropic Enables Self-Service Data Analytics with Claude. Hawker’s point was who wrote it. Not a consultancy selling data governance, not an MDM vendor: the company that builds the model, trying to get its own analytics agents to stop giving wrong answers. And where did they end up? At data foundations. So that’s two of us, from very different vantage points, and a third from inside the model.

It’s a product article too. It sits on Anthropic’s site, filed under Claude Code, and the jump it reports comes from a feature they sell. But look at what the feature does. Skills don’t make the model smarter; they tell it which tables are canonical, who owns which definition and what to read first. Without them, their own model never got past 21% on their evals. With them, it stays above 95%. A model company telling you the model alone isn’t enough is worth more than a data vendor telling you the same.

Two disclosures before I recommend it. I’m a consultant who makes a living from data foundations, and I write these posts with Claude. Discount accordingly. Even so: if you work with data and generative AI, this article is required reading. It isn’t new. It’s the clearest field report I’ve seen on what an agent needs before you can trust it.

What they found

They name three failures. The first, which they call “by far the most common”, is that the agent can’t map a business concept to the single correct table. The second is staleness: sources, definitions and schemas change, and the agent’s knowledge quietly falls behind. The third is retrieval: the right answer is in the model, documented, and the agent simply doesn’t find it.

The finding I keep going back to is an experiment. They gave the agent grep access to thousands of SQL files – dashboards, transformations, analysts’ notebooks – every piece of prior work they had. Accuracy moved less than a point. Their conclusion: “our bottleneck wasn’t access to prior work, it was structure.”

More access didn’t help. Naming things did.

They also test like engineers: evals pinned to a snapshot date so the answer can’t drift under them, and no domain goes live until its agent clears a threshold (they started at about 90%). That’s data quality with a different name. It deserves its own post, and I’ll leave it out of this one.

The same stack, in our vocabulary

Here’s the part the speakers saw and I agree with: almost nothing in the article is new to data management. It just doesn’t use our words. Below is the map. The third column is where I wrote about it from the human side, in Trust Erosion. The fourth is where I’ll write about it from the agent’s side, in the series that starts next week.

What Anthropic calls it What data management calls it Trust Erosion (the human reader) Who Decided That? (the agent reader)
Concept-entity ambiguity Business glossary, metadata, master data False Semantic Consensus · The Table Is Not the Concept · Your Glossary Isn’t Semantics The agent that picks the table by its name
Canonical datasets, the agent “structurally routed to them first” System of record, trusted source The Number Without Perimeter Authority as an eligibility rule, not a ranking signal
Data staleness: accuracy drifted from ~95% to ~65% over a month Metadata currency – –
Deprecated models in the lineage graph ROT data, retirement – Why nobody deletes, and why the old table still competes
LLM-generated metric definitions that “encoded the very ambiguities we were trying to eliminate” Metadata stewardship The Metric as Mirror, Not Window One AI documents, another AI chooses
A provenance footer: source tier, freshness, owner Lineage, data owner The Number Without Perimeter When the agent is wrong, who answers
Business context: a knowledge graph of docs, roadmaps and decision logs Business metadata – Who Decided That?: the whole series
Harvesting every stakeholder correction into a fix for the domain owner Issue management, data quality The Discipline of Distrust When the agent is wrong, who answers

Notice the decision logs. Anthropic had to write down who decided what, so the agent could read it. Hugo knows nothing about your business because, in most companies, those decisions were never written anywhere.

Look at the last row, because it’s the one that settles my problem with Hugo. Anthropic kept the better reader. A scheduled agent scans their stakeholder channels every few hours for people correcting an answer, drafts a one-line fix to the documentation, and opens a pull request tagged to the person who owns that domain. Look closer, though, and that person is no longer optional. The whole correction loop starts when somebody in that channel reads a well-formatted answer and doesn’t believe it. At 95%, that’s one answer in twenty, and it lands in front of someone who asked precisely because they didn’t want to check. Anthropic didn’t replace the better reader. They made the system depend on one.

Meaning and truth

Hawker’s frame for the whole keynote was two words. Trustworthy AI needs meaning and truth, and in his view the industry is buying the first and forgetting the second. Meaning is what a customer is: does “active customer” mean someone who logged in, or someone under contract? Truth is which customers are real: are these 200 records 200 companies, or 80 wearing new names? You need both. One slide put it bluntly: “Meaning without truth is confusion.”

The fourth session of the day, Your AI Agent Is Confidently Wrong About Your Biggest Customer, turned that into a case. An agent is asked for a brief on a key account. It queries the CRM, the call recordings, the customer success platform, and comes back with a confident, well-formatted answer that would have cost a renewal. It couldn’t tell that four differently named companies were one corporate family, or that seven CRM records were four customers.

I agree with the split. I disagree with two things: the word truth, and the order. Since I’m about to tag him, I’d rather say why than nod along.

My first Trust Erosion post had the mirror image. A chemicals distributor in Costa Rica, about 1,800 records in the customer base, and barely 200 of them were active customers. Every sale in that base had happened and was correctly recorded. By Hawker’s split, the records were true. The count was still wrong, because nobody had decided what a customer was. So I’d add the other half to his slide: truth without meaning is a perfectly clean list of things nobody defined.

Then the order. Hawker’s build path goes from identity resolution to shared business concepts. I’d go the other way, and the fourth session’s own case is why. Is “four differently named companies are one customer” a fact about the records, or a decision about the definition? It depends on whether your customer is the legal entity that signs the invoice or the corporate family that negotiates the renewal. Match those records before you decide, and the algorithm decides for you. You can’t resolve the identity until you’ve settled the meaning. In the distributor, the definition of an active customer came first, and nobody had deduplicated anything yet.

That’s why I’d call the second layer identity, not truth. DAMA’s own master data chapter warns that “golden record” is a misleading term and prefers trusted source: a source you’ve decided to trust, not one that holds the truth. Truth sounds like something you discover. Identity is something somebody decides, and writes down, and answers for.

(We agree on the layers and on his main point: without identity, the agent fails. We disagree on the name of one and on which you build first.)

The lesson: meaning comes first, identity second, and both are decisions before they’re data.

What I think is missing

The article is honest about its context, so this isn’t a criticism of what they built. It’s a list of what that context gave them and yours probably won’t.

They have one repository. Nearly all their data code – models, semantic layer, documentation, dashboards – lives together, and about 90% of their data-model changes update the agent’s documentation in the same pull request. Your logic probably lives in an ERP you don’t own and in code nobody has read in years. I’ve just watched an agent build a whole model on the wrong table, and the table’s name was the reason. That story gets its own post.

They have a mandate. Their governance, in their words, “only holds if the canonical models and metric definitions are enforced by tooling (the agent is structurally routed to them first), by CI, and by mandate.” Somebody at Anthropic could say: this is the table, use it. In most companies I work with, nobody has the authority to say that, or nobody wants to spend it.

They deprecate, but the article never says they delete. Their lineage graph tells the agent which models are deprecated. That’s good, and it’s more than most companies do. But a deprecated table is still a table. It still answers to its name, and the next agent, or the next analyst with a notebook, can still find it. Marking something old is a decision anyone can make. Deleting it needs an owner.

They list access controls and data privacy among the design questions and stop there. Two questions the next agent will raise stay open: what it should never have been allowed to read, and what happens when a document it reads gives it an order.

Then there’s the vocabulary. They rebuilt master data, metadata management and data quality and called them canonical datasets, reference docs and evals. That’s fine for Anthropic. For your CFO it can be expensive: reading it, they may not recognize that the governance budget they keep postponing is their AI readiness budget.

Somebody decided

Here’s what the article proves, I think, without meaning to. Anthropic’s agents reach 95% because somebody decided: which table is canonical, who owns each definition, where a correction goes, what the agent reads first. The model didn’t make those decisions. People did, and wrote them down.

Now ask the same question about your data. Who decided that the old sales table would stay? Who wrote the description the agent reads? Who approved what it can see? Who answers when it’s wrong?

In most companies, the answer to all four is the same. Nobody.

That’s the next series. It’s called Who Decided That?, ten posts in four parts: the ROT data the agent competes with, deciding what to keep, what the model reads, and who answers. The cloud and AI made it cheap to create, copy and keep data. They didn’t make it any cheaper to decide.

Trust Erosion asked who reads the number. This one asks who decided what the agent reads.

Before you point an agent at your data

Five questions. If you can’t answer one, that’s where to start.

  1. For the domain you want the agent in, how many canonical datasets do you have, and who declared them canonical?
  2. For each metric the agent will use, is the owner a person or “the team”?
  3. What share of the agent’s answers go through your semantic model rather than raw tables?
  4. When someone corrects the agent, where does that correction go? If the answer is “the chat history”, it goes nowhere.
  5. Who in your company can mandate that the canonical table is the one everybody uses?

Anthropic’s own advice for starting from zero is short: a handful of canonical datasets, a few dozen evals, and a thin layer of documentation the agent reads first. None of that is a model problem.
